title: Intent Engine: LLM-driven query understanding with teacher-student distillation
problem: Legacy query understanding struggled with broad queries, noisy labels, tail queries and fragmented models; rewrites covered about half of search traffic.
depth: Detailed architecture, latency engineering and metrics; teacher model unnamed
facts: Strategy: start from LLMs and inject company context via RAG, validate with guardrails, then fine-tune.
An offline teacher pipeline with caching handles head queries and produces training data; a smaller fine-tuned student serves tail queries in real time.
Out-of-the-box latency was close to 700 ms on A100; merging LoRA adapters and moving to H100 reached about 300 ms.
FP8 quantisation cut latency roughly 10% but reduced recall, so unquantised serving was chosen.
Caching means only about 2% of queries need real-time inference.
Reported results include rewrite coverage above 95% with precision above 90%, and a 50% drop in complaints about poor tail-query results.
interpretations: Splitting offline quality from online latency is the key architectural idea: spend frontier-model cost where latency does not matter, distil for where it does.

decisions.selected: Offline large-model teacher plus distilled small student
decisions.alternatives: Call a frontier model online for every query; classical models only
decisions.reasoning: Source cites latency and cost constraints at search scale.

decisions.alternatives: Trust model output; human review of all outputs

decisions.reasoning: Source states a recall loss outweighed ~10% latency gain.

review_exercise: The post cites a 30% latency gain in one place while its numbers imply a bigger change. How would you reconcile before presenting this to a client?
lessons: Fine-tuning is for behaviour and consistency here, with RAG supplying knowledge.
adaptation: Relevant to SAP Commerce search and B2B catalogue query understanding. Independent analysis.
